items.excerpt: 31 October 2026• Update: 31 October 2026 ... Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start Saturday, including Polish President Karol Nawrocki aborting an Africa trip and returning to Warsaw as a power struggle erupts over control of the Constitutional Tribunal; Türkiye formally nominating OSCE Secretary-General Feridun Sinirlioglu as a candidate for UN secretary-general; and the US State Department approving a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 MSE missiles to Ukraine. Polish President Karol Nawrocki aborted a flight to Senegal and returned to Warsaw as rival groups of judges disputed control of the Constitutional Tribunal, after orders appeared on its website to temporarily remove its president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and vice president Bartlomiej Sochanski, in a move the tribunal rejected as illegal and a "coup." Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska said she ordered the two to stop their duties, while police said they were deployed for possible threats to judges and had not entered the building. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said "restoring the rule of law is our duty," while opposition Law and Justice leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski called the events a "coup against the Constitutional Tribunal." Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski defended the police action as aimed at letting duly elected judges resume the court’s work, while US Ambassador Tom Rose urged restraint, calling the situation "very serious." ... ## US approves $2.1B Patriot missile sale to Ukraine The US State Department approved a possible sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement missiles and related equipment to Ukraine at an estimated cost of $2.1 billion, saying the cost is "funded entirely by partners and allies" and that "no US funds are involved in this sale." Ukraine will pay with donations from Canada, Germany and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, according to the agency, with Lockheed Martin as principal contractor. The approval comes days after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine has received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors per month from the US this year, while needing to intercept around 150 Russian ballistic missiles per month. ... - Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez acknowledged that "trust in high-speed rail has been shattered" after a collision near Urda killed at least 69 people earlier this week, the country's second major high-speed rail disaster this year.

items.title: PCE inflation report September 2026:
items.excerpt: Published Thu, Oct 29 2026 8:32 AM EDT Updated Thu, Oct 29 2026 2:06 PM EDT ... - Inflation continued to run above the Fed's 2% target in September, with a headline rate of 3.6% and core at 3.1%, according to the central bank's preferred gauge. ... The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends. While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter. GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter. Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%. The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move. "The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that's happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday. However, the data deluge from Thursday shows the Fed could have more work to do. ... Consumer spending rose 3.8% in the third quarter, the same pace as the prior period. Gross private domestic investment soared 19.4%, driven by a 20.9% surge in equipment spending and an 8.4% jump on intellectual property products. ... There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%. At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

items.title: U.S. Inflation Accelerates as AI Investment Relies More on Debt | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: By Adrian Vale Oct 31, 2026, 1:36 PM UTC Updated Oct 31, 2026, 1:36 PM UTC 3 min read ... U.S. inflation accelerated in September as artificial-intelligence investment increasingly relied on debt, putting price pressures and financing risks in focus for investors and policymakers ahead of two November inflation releases. Bloomberg News reported Oct. 31 that a roundup of views from nine financial professionals examined risks spanning inflation, AI financing and wealth concentration. The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose 3.6% over the 12 months through September, while its measure excluding food and energy rose 3.1%. The two indexes increased 0.5% and 0.3%, respectively, from August. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported that the separate Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7% over the year and 0.6% from August on a seasonally adjusted basis. Gasoline prices climbed 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the monthly CPI increase. CPI and PCE use different methods and baskets. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) put its median PCE inflation projection at 2.3% in 2027, measured from the fourth quarter of 2026 to the fourth quarter of 2027. Participants’ forecasts ranged from 2.0% to 2.6% and depend on their assessments of appropriate monetary policy. In a separate report, the BLS said final-demand prices rose 1.3% in September from August on a seasonally adjusted basis. Processed materials excluding food and energy rose 8.5% over the year, while unprocessed nonfood materials excluding energy rose 24.3%. ... The next scheduled inflation readings are the October CPI release on Nov. 10 at 8:30 a.m. ET and the October PCE price index on Nov. 25 at 8:30 a.m. EST.

items.title: Inflation heats up again, days before midterm elections | PBS News
items.excerpt: Economy Oct 29, 2026 12:24 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — An inflation gauge closely monitored by the Federal Reserve accelerated last month, showing that prices remain elevated less than a week before midterm elections in which the uncomfortably high cost of living for millions of Americans has become a central issue. Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May. Rising gas prices drove much of the inflation increase as renewed violence in the Middle East has kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, up from below $70 before the Iran war. But prices also rose outside of fuel costs. items.excerpt: A federal judge issued a sweeping order Friday night blocking the Trump administration from threatening or intimidating election officials amid pressure tactics used by the administration in the weeks leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The eight-page order prohibits any action that may “threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers to demand that they halt processing the ballots of any registered voter solely on the basis that the ballot belongs to an individual alleged by [the administration] to be ineligible to vote.” “In the lead-up to the election, high-ranking DOJ and DHS officials have engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election,” wrote U.S. ... “Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” Thompson wrote Friday. The judge’s order extends through Nov. 16, nearly two weeks after Election Day.

items.title: US campaign for control of Congress enters final weekend
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Oct 31 (Reuters) - The Trump administration pressed a criminal investigation into Alaska's pivotal US Senate race and said on Saturday it would likely take its fight over thousands of California mail-in ballots to the Supreme Court, as the midterm campaign for control of Congress entered its final weekend. In ‌Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola helped to recruit a retired schoolteacher, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to run because he shares a name with ‌the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan. The closely contested race is seen as crucial to Democrats' hopes of taking the Senate in Tuesday's vote. It is one of 35 Senate races, along with all 435 House seats, that will decide whether ​Trump's Republicans keep control of Congress for his final two years in office. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a narrow edge in the House. Losing either chamber would let Democrats block Trump's agenda and launch investigations of an administration that has until now faced largely compliant Republican majorities. Early voting has set a record. More than 51 million Americans have already cast ballots in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day at the last midterms in 2022. In California, a federal appeals court earlier this week ruled 2-1 that the Justice Department had failed to ‌justify its emergency bid to force the state to set aside mail ⁠ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are likely noncitizens. "I hesitate to give a final answer, but I think probably the Supreme Court's next on this one," acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told Fox News on Saturday, adding that any request for Supreme Court consideration would come before Tuesday's election. Trump has ⁠been on a campaign blitz in multiple states over the past month but is spending Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. He returns to the campaign trail on Sunday in Kansas and Iowa. ALASKA PROBE INTENSIFIES The US Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a Friday press conference that a recent New York Times article saying there had been an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had ​driven ​a "surge" of FBI resources onto the case. Heyman said he had assigned several prosecutors to it and that investigative steps ​were taking place "intensely and swiftly." The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Peltola ‌aides worked with staff at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to recruit Sullivan Jr. Heyman called him a "sham candidate" but declined to say what crime may have been committed. Peltola and the campaign committee have denied involvement in any effort to recruit the second Sullivan. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign. The department had already filed its civil action but, Heyman said, "when the New York Times article hit, that's additional information that accelerated what we've been doing." MICHIGAN RIFT In Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in another closely watched Senate race, El-Sayed's feud with the rival he beat in the primary, US Representative Haley Stevens, flared again. El-Sayed's campaign asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as "not to distract from the central issues of the campaign," a person familiar with the matter said. Stevens ‌has backed El-Sayed but demanded he condemn an outside group's ad blaming Israel for high grocery prices and apologize ​for past rhetoric about Israel. "It's certainly unhelpful to the El-Sayed campaign to have continued visible division within the party just ​before Election Day," said Matt Grossman, a political scientist at Michigan State University. Polls show ​El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support. TRUMP'S PRESSURE CAMPAIGN ON STATES The administration, beyond its bid to block counting of ballots from more than 20,000 California voters it alleges ‌could be noncitizens, has sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia ​seeking unredacted voter rolls. The legal maneuvers have alarmed ​state election officials. Under the Constitution, states have primary authority over how elections are run. On Friday, a federal judge ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening to prosecute California election officials who defy its directives. Sean Morales-Doyle of the Brennan Center for Justice said the efforts, while unlikely to win in court, aim at "creating uncertainty, sowing fear, distrust, chaos," in hopes of pressuring ​officials such as Alaska's lieutenant governor "to do something that they're not supposed ‌to do." Even so, 76% of US voters are confident their ballots will be counted accurately, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from September 30 to October 5, with confidence about ​equally high among Republicans and Democrats.

items.excerpt: - AP - Oct 31, 2026 - Oct 31, 2026 Updated 10 hrs ago Houdini’s centennial spotlight: A newly published essay and a fresh fight over when and how he died NEW YORK (AP) — Harry Houdini, a century after his death, continues to captivate. A rare essay by the escape artist has been published, shedding light on his early influences. A recent book revisits questions about the cause and date of his death. Houdini, born Erik Weisz, became an international celebrity known for his escape acts. His mysterious death on Halloween 1926 remains debated, with new theories challenging the official cause. Centennial events this weekend include a "Grand Houdini Centenarium" in Budapest, an auction in Hollywood, and seances in Chicago and Maryland. Despite the intrigue, experts say his legacy endures through his remarkable life. Scott Clifton and Tamara Tunie earn lead acting Daytime Emmys. 'General Hospital' wins again LOS ANGELES (AP) — Scott Clifton of “The Bold and the Beautiful” and Tamara Tunie of “Beyond the Gates” have won lead acting honors at the Daytime Emmy Awards. It's Clifton's second career trophy in the lead category. Tunie made her return to the soap opera genre after 17 years away. “General Hospital” won its record 19th trophy overall as outstanding drama and sixth in a row. Roger Howarth and Beth Maitland of “The Young and the Restless” swept the supporting acting categories. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, lost in the lifestyle program category for her former Netflix show “With Love, Meghan.” Margaret Qualley, Jack Antonoff file for divorce after 3 years of marriage NEW YORK (AP) — Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage. Court records show the case was filed Friday in Kings County Supreme Court in New York as an uncontested matrimonial action. Qualley is listed as the plaintiff, and Antonoff as the defendant. The couple separated in July. Qualley, 32, is known for films like “The Substance” and “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Antonoff, 42, is a 14-time Grammy-winning songwriter and producer. The couple began dating in 2021 and married in August 2023. An introspective Kirk Franklin is no longer apologizing with 'I Am What I Am' album NEW YORK (AP) — Kirk Franklin is back with his new album, "I Am What I Am," out Friday. His 14th studio project and first double album, 14 tracks are divided between contemporary music and traditional, live-recorded gospel songs. Features include gospel royalty Karen Clark Sheard and star mainstream artists like Jelly Roll, Davido and GloRilla. “This Time," featuring GloRilla, hit No. 1 on Billboard’s hot gospel songs, extending Franklin's record to ten No. 1s on the chart. Known for his crossover hits, the 20-time Grammy winner has frequently faced criticism for working with secular artists, but remains unapologetic in the name of spreading his Christian faith. ... The Shakespearean actor in 1987 became Capt. Jean-Luc Picard, the unlikely and poetic face of that show’s sequel, “Star Trek: The Next Generation.” For a fan base that has long signed on as acolytes of a brighter, more equitable future, recent days have made the present sting. ... (AP) — Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her. The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office filed paperwork Thursday to drop a felony charge of battery by strangulation because of “insufficient evidence.” Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, still faces a misdemeanor charge of battery domestic violence. Ross has pleaded not guilty to all charges. Officials say Ross surrendered at the Miami Beach police station on Oct. 1, two days after the woman filed a report with police.
